answer: DeepWalk treats the random walks generated over the graph as a corpus of 'sentences', where each vertex visited in a walk is a 'word'. From this corpus it builds a vocabulary V, which is simply the set of graph vertices (each vertex v in V is a unique word, so the vocabulary size equals the number of vertices |V|). Vertex identities are mapped to word tokens, and the vocabulary is not a separate set of learned language words. During training, DeepWalk feeds these walk sequences into a skip-gram language model (Word2Vec-style, typically with hierarchical softmax) that learns a latent representation Φ: v -> R^{|V|×d} for each vertex. Because the vertices form their own vocabulary, the model learns one embedding per vertex, with the context of each vertex defined by the vertices appearing within a window of size w around it in the walks. The vertex embeddings are the only parameters of interest and are used as the node representations, while the context (output) side of the skip-gram model is auxiliary.
